Base directory for this skill: /Users/ben/github/toulmin/evals/toulmin/variants/questions-only/skills/toulmin

# Writing the piece

Before you write, ask the user for what you are missing. The user's request is never everything the user knows. Send one message with at most six questions, the most useful first. Ask only what would change the piece and what the request does not already answer. Look for these:

- **What the reader gets and what it costs them.** The terms as they touch this reader: pay, price, dates, what they keep, what they lose, what they can still do if they change their mind.
- **What answers the reader's main objection.** Name the objection this reader will raise and ask what the user has that answers it: what has already been done or offered about it, what has changed since, what the proposal leaves in place.
- **What shows the writer can deliver, or knows the reader's world.** A record, a credential, a time they did this before, someone who has checked their work or will vouch for it.
- **What the writer can commit to.** A date, a number, a named person, what happens if it is missed.
- **The reader.** Who exactly reads this, what they already think of the writer, and anything they hold against the writer, when the request does not say.
- **The names and dates the piece cannot go out without.** Who it is addressed to, who signs it, a deadline.
- **What the reader will find out anyway.** Close with one open question: is there a cost, a limit, a weak number or a past failure that the request leaves out and this reader knows or will learn?

When the answers come back, write the piece as you normally would, and hand it over. When the user does not know something, write without it and do not guess.


ARGUMENTS: Staff email from a partner at a 46-person architecture firm announcing end of fully remote work: in office Tue/Wed/Thu from September 1; 15 hired fully remote in 2021-22, 4 live 2+ hours away and can stay remote until end of next year then come in once a week; lost two hospital projects at final interview, clients said team seemed not to know each other; juniors hired since 2022 take ~30% longer to lead a project; partners have been in one day a week and will now be in all three days. One page, goes before Friday all-staff meeting.

Before I draft this, a few questions. Your answers will change what the email says.

1. **What do the other 11 remote hires get?** They live within two hours, so they go from fully remote to three days a week. Is there any help for them, such as travel costs, a transition period or flexible start times? Is there an exception process for caregiving, health or disability? Those 11 will read this email most closely, so I need to know what they keep.
2. **Do their contracts say "remote"?** If the offer letters for the 15 named remote as a term, this email may need to say how that will be handled, for example individual conversations or revised agreements. Has anyone checked?
3. **Can Monday and Friday stay remote?** And is the office ready for everyone on the same three days? Do you have enough desks, meeting rooms and quiet space? If people come in and there's nowhere to sit, the case falls apart.
4. **Dates.** Today is November 16, 2026, so I'm reading this as September 1, 2027, with the four distant staff remote until December 31, 2027 and then in once a week from January 2028. Is that right?
5. **How firm is the 30% figure?** Staff hired in 2022 were brought on during a strange period, and some will say that explains the gap. Is there anything else behind it, like mentoring that didn't happen or feedback from the juniors themselves? Or should I present it as what your review records show and leave it there?
6. **Who signs, and what happens on Friday?** Is it from you alone or all three partners? Will Friday be a chance for questions, with the details still open, or is it settled?

One more: is there anything staff already know or will find out that cuts against this? For example, a promise made when you hired the remote staff, a recent office move or lease decision, or people who have already said they'd leave.

<final_document>
**Subject: Office days from September 1, 2027**

Everyone,

From September 1, 2027, everyone at the firm will work in the office on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. Monday and Friday stay remote. I want to explain why before we meet on Friday.

**Why we're doing this**

Last year we reached the final interview for two large hospital projects and lost both. Both clients told us the same thing: our team seemed not to know each other. That's the kind of work we most want to win, and we lost it because of how we came across as a team.

The second reason is about people who've joined recently. Our review records show that junior staff hired since 2022 are taking about 30% longer to reach the point where they lead a project. Five of our six project leads already come in three days a week by choice. Juniors who work mostly from home get less time alongside them, and we think that's part of the gap.

This applies to the partners too. We've been coming in one day a week, which is less than we're now asking of you. From September, all three of us will be in on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.

**For those of you hired as remote**

Fifteen of you joined in 2021 and 2022 as fully remote employees. This is a real change to the job you took on, and I won't pretend otherwise.

- The four of you who live more than two hours from the office can keep working remotely until December 31, 2027. From January 2028, you'll come in one day a week.
- Everyone else will work the three office days from September 1.
- Those four are the only exceptions. I know some of you will have hoped for more, and I'd rather tell you that now than on Friday.

**What we're putting in place**

- Anyone who lives more than 30 miles from the office will get up to $150 a month toward commuting.
- We don't have a desk for everyone yet. New desks arrive in August, before the change starts.
- The policy is decided, but it isn't fixed forever. Six months in, we'll review with all of you how it's working.

**Friday**

We'll meet at 10 a.m. on Friday in the main studio. If you'd like to raise something before then, come to me or to HR. I'd rather hear it now than have you sit on it.

Paul Whitaker
Partner
</final_document>

Two things to check before sending:

- **Contracts.** Nobody has checked whether the offer letters for the 15 remote hires list remote work as a term. If they do, changing it may need each person's agreement. That would change how the "For those of you hired as remote" section should read. I'd have HR or your employment lawyer check before Friday.
- **"Only exceptions."** Depending on where you are, you may be legally required to consider individual requests on disability or similar grounds, whatever the policy says. Even if you expect to grant none, it may be safer to replace "Those four are the only exceptions" with something like "Apart from those four, the three days apply to everyone." That way the email doesn't promise to refuse every request.

I also left out how to claim the $150 commuting money because you didn't say. If HR has the process ready, one line on it would help.
